qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture eleven. Flocking. This is how a few simple rules make a flock, with no leader.
Fifty birds fly as one flock, and nobody leads them.
A flock moves as one, with no leader.
A predator strikes the middle. The nearest birds swerve away, and the flock breaks up.
A predator strikes: nearby birds swerve away.
Then the groups find each other again, with no one in charge.
Then the flock pulls back together.
One body length apart is too close. Repulsion pushes the two birds apart.
Too close: the two birds push apart.
Six lengths apart is too far. Attraction pulls them together.
Too far: they pull together.
At about three lengths, push and pull cancel, and the pair holds steady.
In between, the two urges cancel out.
Reynolds called his simulated birds boids. A boid senses only the flockmates near it.
A boid only senses flockmates nearby.
With a radius of eighty, four flockmates fall inside.
Inside its radius: 4 flockmates.
For each one, it knows the distance and the direction. The nearest is forty-five away, a little to its left.
It knows each one's distance and direction.
It senses all round, so a flockmate behind it still counts.
It sees all round, even behind it.
Rule one is separation. Closer than twenty, a flockmate is too close.
Rule 1, separation: don't crowd.
The closer it is, the harder it pushes. Five away pushes zero point seven five, and twenty-five away pushes nothing.
The closer a flockmate, the harder the push.
So the boid steers away from the close one.
So the boid steers away.
Soon nobody is within twenty.
Now nobody is too close.
Rule two is alignment. The boid turns to match its neighbours.
Rule 2, alignment: match your neighbours.
It heads north, and its four neighbours head east.
On average, its neighbours head east.
Each step, it turns part of the way towards their average heading.
It turns a little towards them each step.
Soon all five head the same way, and polarisation reaches one.
Soon they all head the same way.
Rule three is cohesion. The boid stays with its group.
Rule 3, cohesion: stay with the group.
It finds the centre of its neighbours. Most of them are on its right.
It finds the centre of its neighbours.
So it steers right, towards that centre.
And steers towards that centre.
Everyone does the same, and the group closes up.
The group closes up.
Each tick, a boid adds its three pushes. Separation, alignment and cohesion.
Each boid adds up its three pushes.
The sum is one arrow, and it turns the boid.
The sum turns it.
All forty boids do this at once, each using only its own neighbours.
All boids do this at the same time.
The scattered crowd becomes one flock, all heading one way, with no leader.
Out of the chaos, one flock forms.
Start sixty boids packed together, and separation flings them apart. The spread grows about ten times.
Start them packed: they burst apart.
Then cohesion and alignment pull them back into a flock.
Then they gather again.
Now two flocks fly straight at each other.
Two flocks meet head-on.
They merge, and fly on as one flock.
They join and fly on as one flock.
A boid is a tiny agent. An agent senses its world through sensors.
An agent senses its world with sensors.
What it senses right now is its percept. Here, four flockmates, the nearest one forty away on its right.
What it senses right now is its percept.
Then it acts through actuators. For a boid, the action is a turn. This tick, it turns right six degrees.
Then it acts with actuators: here, a turn.
The others move too, so the world changes, and it senses again.
The others move too, so it senses again.
A multi-agent system has many agents working together. Here there are ten.
Many agents can work together.
If all ten talk to each other, that takes forty-five links.
If all 10 talk to each other: 45 links.
Talking only to neighbours takes just ten links, so it scales.
Talking only to neighbours: 10 links.
One agent turns faulty. A central monitor watches for faults.
One central monitor watches for faults.
If the monitor breaks, the fault spreads until all ten are infected. That is a single point of failure.
If it breaks, one bad agent infects them all.
A flock has no leader, only simple local rules.
Separation, alignment and cohesion add up to one turn.
An agent senses its world, then acts, again and again.
